after_evaluation.answer_quote: To avoid repeated losses for urgent or schedule-constrained residents, 10% of Open Pool blocks are reserved for urgent/essential use and recurring schedule windows, allocated by lottery among eligible applicants, and any resident who loses two consecutive Open Pool draws receives one priority ticket in the next draw.
after_evaluation.conclusion: answered provisionally yes: the reserve and carryover are derived as access measures for urgent or schedule-constrained residents, subject to the stated falsifier that they must not crowd out newcomers or increase unused bookings
after_evaluation.derivation: Read from AFTER ANSWER, this step adds two operative components to the Open Pool: (i) a bounded reserve of 10% of Open Pool blocks allocated by lottery among eligible urgent/essential and recurring-schedule applicants, and (ii) a consecutive-loss carryover granting one priority ticket in the next draw after two consecutive losses. The return states the rationale directly — to avoid repeated losses for urgent or schedule-constrained residents — and ties each component to exactly the access condition the question names: the reserve addresses urgent and schedule-constrained access, and the carryover addresses repeated lottery loss. The same step carries a public falsifier for the second half of the question: the additions would be contradicted if they failed to improve access for urgent or schedule-constrained residents without crowding out newcomers or increasing unused bookings. AFTER ANSWER also propagates the change: step 5, step 11 and the working-position claim all now name the bounded access reserve and consecutive-loss carryover, and the trial metrics add bounded access wait time, consecutive-loss rate, and urgent-reserve use. So the return supplies a reason that is substantive for this question rather than merely relabelling the bookkeeping string: it changes the Open Pool's eligibility and ticket structure in a way aimed at the exact access gap, and states the condition under which the change would fail.

before_evaluation.answer_quote: The Open Pool is allocated by lottery: every resident gets one base ticket per block; a newcomer gets a one-time guaranteed first-use token and, for the first three bookings, one extra ticket; anyone who has not used the workshop in 90 days gets one extra ticket.
before_evaluation.conclusion: undecided at BEFORE ANSWER: the Open Pool has no reserve or carryover component, so the question has no answering derivation in that state (not a substantive negative answer)
before_evaluation.derivation: Read from BEFORE ANSWER, the Open Pool mechanism has exactly three ticket components: one base ticket per resident per block, a one-time newcomer first-use token with one extra ticket for the first three bookings, and one extra ticket for anyone unused for 90 days. No block is carved out ahead of the lottery for urgent or essential use, no recurring schedule window is protected, and no rule rewards a resident who has lost repeated draws. Therefore BEFORE ANSWER supplies no derivation that any bounded reserve or consecutive-loss carryover raises access for urgent or schedule-constrained residents, and it likewise supplies no derivation about whether such a reserve would crowd out newcomers or leave bookings unused, because the mechanism contains no such component to analyse. On the question as posed, BEFORE ANSWER has no operative step and leaves it undecided rather than answering it in the negative.

dependency.after_quote: My working position is that the town should adopt a two-pool rolling allocation with equal-chance lotteries for open slots plus a small bounded access reserve and consecutive-loss carryover, a published rubric for milestone-based project priority, progressive release and standby filling of unused project blocks, and public adaptive review.
dependency.before_quote: My working position is that the town should adopt a two-pool rolling allocation with equal-chance lotteries for open slots, milestone-based priority for project slots, automatic release of unused project blocks, and public adaptive review, because this balances newcomer access, project completion, high utilization, and challengeability under uncertain demand and strategic booking.
dependency.explanation: The later answer to this question depends on a substantive reason supplied by the return, and the dependence is identifiable from content rather than from string bookkeeping. The before working position commits only to equal-chance lotteries for open slots; its Open Pool has base tickets, a temporary newcomer or returning-user boost, and nothing else, so the question of whether a reserve and carryover improve urgent or schedule-constrained access has no answering step in it. The after working position adds 'plus a small bounded access reserve and consecutive-loss carryover,' and step 5 of the after answer grounds that addition in a reason aimed at this very question ('to avoid repeated losses for urgent or schedule-constrained residents') together with an explicit refutation condition. That added reason, not the mere difference between the two committed strings, is what converts an undecided question into a provisional yes. A reader could have a different position that dropped the reserve and carryover while keeping the same bookkeeping relation intact, and could keep the same working position string while disputing the access rationale; so the dependence is on the reason, and equality or difference of the working_position strings neither establishes nor rules out this substantive dependence. Note also that the after answer offers no derivation quantifying the crowding-out or utilization effects, so the dependence is on a reason that is substantive for access but still unfalsified in practice.

problem_derivation: From the PROBLEM alone, the only derivation available is over the four stated goals under the explicitly acknowledged unknown demand and strategic booking: newcomers must get a fair chance, experienced users must complete demanding projects, few bookings must go unused, and rules must be understandable and challengeable. The PROBLEM contains no reserve, carryover, lottery-weight, or loss-streak construct, and it fixes no demand level, so no step in it entails that any particular reserve percentage or carryover rule would raise urgent access rather than substitute for newcomer chances or leave reserved blocks idle. The conjunction of unknown demand and unknown strategic response makes the targeted question underdetermined at PROBLEM: an answer could only be added by importing a premise the PROBLEM does not supply.
question: Does the town's adoption of the bounded access reserve plus consecutive-loss carryover (10% of Open Pool blocks reserved for urgent/essential and recurring schedule-window use, and a priority ticket after two consecutive Open Pool losses) improve access for urgent or schedule-constrained residents without crowding out newcomers or increasing unused bookings?
